text: From that time on, no one tried to remove the veil, and Mister Hooper became a man apart, for people avoided him and children fled at his approach. <break time="0.8s" /> Hating the veil himself, he never passed a mirror nor stooped to drink at a still fountain, lest he should be frightened by his own reflection. <break time="0.8s" /> Gossips whispered that some great crime lay hidden behind the black crape, and a cloud of sin or sorrow seemed to wrap the poor minister wherever he went. <break time="0.8s" /> Yet the veil had one desirable effect, for it made him a very efficient clergyman with awful power over souls that were in agony for sin. <break time="0.8s" /> Dying sinners called for Mister Hooper and would not breathe their last until he appeared, though they always shuddered when the veiled face bent over them. <break time="0.8s" /> Once, under Governor Belcher, he preached the election sermon, and his words made so deep an impression that the laws of that year were full of gloom and piety. <break time="0.8s" /> In this manner Mister Hooper spent a long life, kind and loving though unloved, shunned in times of joy but always summoned in times of mortal anguish. <break time="0.8s" /> As years wore on, shedding their snows above his black veil, he won a name throughout the New England churches, and people called him Father Hooper.
